welcome.source_title: Welcome to Ischys Integrative Mental Wellness

blocks.text: Taking care of your mental health isn't about becoming a different person. It's about understanding what is happening, discovering what helps, and finding ways to help you function and feel better in your everyday life.
At Ischys Integrative Mental Wellness, we believe good psychiatric care starts by looking at the whole person—not just a diagnosis or a list of symptoms.
Medication may be an important part of your treatment, but it is rarely the entire picture.
Sleep, nutrition, movement, physical health, relationships, stress, substances, hormones, daily routines, meaningful activities, and your environment can all influence how you feel and function.
That's why we'll look at the bigger picture together.
That means I want to know not only what symptoms you're experiencing, but also:
What is getting in the way of the life you want to live?
What changes feel realistic right now?

Treatment may include psychiatric medication, education, behavioral strategies, lifestyle interventions, collaboration with your therapist or other healthcare providers, and evidence-informed integrative approaches when appropriate.
Most importantly, you have a voice in your treatment.
I will explain the reasoning behind recommendations, discuss alternatives when they exist, and help you understand the potential benefits and risks so that we can make thoughtful decisions together.
Think of it as a collection of tools.
Some will be useful now. Others may become useful later. You don't need to change everything at once, and you certainly don't need to do everything perfectly.
Inside, we'll explore things such as:
Sleep • Movement • Nutrition • Hobbies • Relationships • Stress • Coping Skills • Substances •
You may be surprised by how much seemingly small changes can influence the way you feel.
Mental health symptoms can make change difficult.
Depression can make getting started feel impossible.
ADHD can make knowing what to do very different from actually doing it.
Anxiety can make change feel overwhelming.
Recovery from substance use can require rebuilding routines, relationships, pleasure, and purpose.
Whatever brought you here, we'll start where you are.
You don't need to fix your whole life this week.
Sometimes the first goal is simply finding one thing that makes tomorrow a little better than today.
A Question to Take With You
If your mental health improved, what would you be able to do—or enjoy—that is difficult for you right now?
Welcome to Ischys Integrative Mental Wellness.
Whole-person psychiatric care. Thoughtful treatment. One step at a time.

This toolkit provides general educational information and does not replace individualized medical or mental health advice. Your treatment recommendations will be based on your individual needs, medical history, symptoms, goals, and circumstances.

hobbies.source_title: Hobbies That Support Mental Health: Finding Something That Helps Your Brain Recharge

blocks.text: Mental wellness isn't only about medication or therapy. What you repeatedly do with your time can influence stress, mood, attention, sleep, confidence, and your sense of connection with other people.
A hobby won't replace treatment for a mental health condition, but meaningful activities can become an important part of taking care of your brain.
The best hobby isn't necessarily the one that's supposed to be "good for mental health." It's one you actually enjoy enough to keep doing.
When we're depressed, anxious, overwhelmed, or burned out, life can gradually become smaller.
We may stop doing things that previously gave us pleasure, accomplishment, connection, or purpose.

Feeling poorly doing less experiencing fewer rewarding moments feeling even worse. → → → Psychotherapy sometimes addresses this through behavioral activation—intentionally bringing meaningful and rewarding activities back into your life rather than waiting until you feel motivated enough to start.
Different hobbies can support mental health in different ways. Some provide physical activity.
Others promote creativity, mastery, mindfulness, social connection, or simply a break from repetitive thinking.
Play an instrument, sing, join a choir, make playlists, attend concerts, or simply listen intentionally.
Music can influence arousal and emotion, making it useful both when you need to settle your nervous system and when you need energy.
You don't need musical talent to benefit from music. The goal isn't performance—it's engagement.
Try: Create three playlists: one for calming down, one for getting moving, and one containing songs that reliably improve your mood.

Walking, hiking, fishing, birdwatching, camping, or simply sitting outside can provide something many of us don't get enough of: movement, daylight, sensory stimulation, and distance from screens and everyday demands.
You don't need to climb a mountain.
A walk through a park counts.
Try: Put your phone away for 10–20 minutes and deliberately notice what you can see, hear, smell, and feel around you.
Gardening combines several potentially beneficial ingredients: movement, sensory experiences, routine, nurturing something over time, and visible evidence of progress.
No yard? Try herbs in the kitchen, a few houseplants, or a community garden.
There is something psychologically powerful about caring for something today that you won't see the full results of until later.
Cooking provides creativity, planning, sensory stimulation, and a tangible reward at the end.
It can also become a social activity. Cook with a partner, teach a child a family recipe, invite someone to dinner, or learn dishes from another culture.
If cooking feels like another chore, however, don't force it into becoming your "self-care." Choose something you genuinely enjoy.
Movement doesn't have to mean going to the gym.
Dancing, yoga, swimming, cycling, martial arts, pickleball, running, walking, or recreational sports can combine physical activity with enjoyment.
Dance has an additional advantage: music, movement, coordination, learning, and sometimes social connection happen simultaneously.
And dancing badly in your kitchen still counts.
Painting, drawing, woodworking, pottery, knitting, crocheting, sewing, jewelry making, model building, scrapbooking, or other hands-on projects can give your attention somewhere productive to go.
Creative hobbies can be especially valuable for people whose minds rarely seem to turn off.
The point isn't whether the finished product is "good."
Creating and performing are two different things. You are allowed to create something without being good at it.
Photography can change the way you pay attention.
Instead of moving automatically through your environment, you begin looking for light, color, expressions, textures, landscapes, and small details you might otherwise miss.
Try a simple challenge: photograph one interesting or beautiful thing every day for a month.
Writing can help organize experiences that feel chaotic when they're only circulating in your head.
Traditional journaling isn't for everyone. Other options include:
writing down three things that went well that day
You don't need to produce pages. Five minutes can be enough.
Yoga, tai chi, qigong, stretching, breathing exercises, and meditation combine attention with awareness of the body.
For some people, sitting still and trying to "clear the mind" is frustrating—particularly when they have ADHD, significant anxiety, or racing thoughts.
The goal isn't to have no thoughts. It's practicing the ability to notice where your attention has gone and gently redirect it.
Sometimes the most therapeutic ingredient isn't the hobby itself—it's connection.
Consider a recreational sports league, running or walking group, choir, book club, gaming group, volunteer organization, church/community activity, crafting group, or class.
This can be particularly useful when depression or anxiety has gradually led to isolation.
You don't have to become highly social. Even regularly being around people who share an interest can create a sense of belonging.
When someone is depressed, one of the symptoms can be anhedonia—a reduced ability to experience pleasure or interest.
That creates a frustrating problem: people are often told to "do something you enjoy" precisely when they don't enjoy anything.
"What could I tolerate doing for 10 minutes?"
Motivation doesn't always come before action. Sometimes action comes first, and motivation gradually follows.
Choosing the Right Hobby for Your Brain
Instead of looking for the single "best" hobby for mental health, think about what may be missing from your life right now.
If you're isolated: choose something involving people.
If you're mentally overstimulated: try nature, gardening, repetitive crafts, or gentle movement.
If you're bored or under-stimulated: consider music, dance, sports, learning, or something challenging.
If you're feeling ineffective or discouraged: choose something that produces visible progress or a finished product.
If you're spending too much time in your head: consider a physical or hands-on activity.
If life feels like nothing but responsibilities: choose something with absolutely no productive purpose other than enjoyment.
You don't have to monetize your hobby, become exceptional at it, post it online, or turn it into another accomplishment.
A Note From Ischys Integrative Mental Wellness

Mental health treatment can include medication and psychotherapy, but wellness is broader than either one. Sleep, movement, relationships, nutrition, meaningful activity, recreation, and connection all contribute to the larger picture.

If depression, anxiety, ADHD, trauma symptoms, or another mental health concern is making it difficult to participate in your life—even in activities you once enjoyed—it may be worth talking with a mental health professional.
Hobbies can support mental health. They aren't a substitute for appropriate mental health care when treatment is needed.
This information is intended for general education and is not a substitute for individualized medical or mental health advice, diagnosis, or treatment.

caffeine.source_title: Caffeine: More Than Just a Morning Pick-Me-Up

blocks.text: Coffee, tea, soda, energy drinks, pre-workout supplements, chocolate, and even some medications can contain caffeine.
For many people, moderate caffeine use causes few problems. But caffeine is still a psychoactive stimulant, which means it affects your brain, nervous system, sleep, and cardiovascular system.
When we're trying to understand your mental health—or determine whether a medication is working—your caffeine intake can be an important piece of the puzzle.
Caffeine primarily works by blocking adenosine, a chemical that builds up throughout the day and helps your brain recognize that it is becoming tired.
Blocking adenosine can temporarily make you feel:
People differ considerably in their sensitivity to caffeine.
There's a reason some people with ADHD are drawn to coffee, soda, or energy drinks: caffeine is stimulating.
Some people report temporarily feeling more alert or focused after caffeine. That doesn't mean caffeine treats ADHD as reliably as established ADHD treatments.
The bigger concern is total stimulant load.
If you take a stimulant medication and also consume significant amounts of caffeine, you may be more likely to experience:
racing heart • elevated blood pressure • jitteriness • anxiety • irritability • tremor • appetite
Sometimes a patient believes their medication dose is too high when caffeine is contributing to the symptoms.
Other times, large amounts of caffeine are being used to compensate for inadequate sleep, untreated symptoms, or medication wearing off.
That's why it's important for your psychiatric provider to know how much caffeine you're actually consuming.
Caffeine can create physical sensations that resemble anxiety:
faster heartbeat • sweating • trembling • restlessness • rapid breathing • feeling "wired"
For someone prone to panic attacks, those physical sensations can sometimes become the beginning of a panic cycle.
If anxiety suddenly becomes worse, caffeine is one of several factors worth examining.
When you're exhausted or depressed, caffeine can feel like a quick solution.
The problem can become a cycle:
Poor sleep fatigue more caffeine poorer sleep more fatigue more caffeine → → → → → Rather than simply adding caffeine, persistent fatigue deserves investigation.
Sleep quality, depression, medications, iron deficiency, thyroid problems, sleep apnea, nutrition, and other medical conditions can all contribute to fatigue.
Caffeine doesn't need to be automatically eliminated during recovery.
However, it's worth paying attention to how it is being used.

For some people, heavy caffeine or energy-drink consumption becomes another way of repeatedly changing how they feel—particularly when boredom, fatigue, stress, cravings, or emotional discomfort appear.
That's something to become curious about rather than ashamed of.
Am I drinking this because I enjoy it—or because I feel like I can't function without it?
Caffeine Can Affect Your Heart Rate and Blood Pressure
Caffeine can temporarily increase heart rate or blood pressure in some people.
This becomes especially relevant when we are also prescribing medications that can affect cardiovascular function.
If we're monitoring your blood pressure or pulse after starting or adjusting a medication, tell us about your caffeine intake.
A blood pressure measurement after an energy drink may tell us something very different from your usual resting blood pressure.
Caffeine can remain active in the body for hours.
You may be able to fall asleep after drinking coffee and still experience poorer sleep quality.
And caffeine isn't only in coffee.
Serving size matters. A large specialty coffee or energy drink may contain considerably more caffeine than you expect.

Those symptoms can sometimes be mistaken for worsening depression, ADHD, or medication side effects.
If you're consuming a lot of caffeine, gradually reducing it may be more comfortable than abruptly stopping.

You don't necessarily need to give up your morning coffee.
We want to understand how much you're using, when you're using it, why you're using it, and how your body responds.
Those details can help us make better decisions about your sleep, anxiety, attention, blood pressure, heart rate, medications, and overall mental wellness.

sleep.source_title: Sleep: Your Brain Needs It More Than You Think

blocks.text: Sleep isn't simply the time when your body shuts down.
While you sleep, your brain is actively regulating systems involved in attention, memory, emotion, stress, appetite, learning, and physical recovery.
That's why one of the questions you'll hear frequently at Ischys is:
It's not small talk. Sleep gives us important information about your mental health.
When Sleep Changes, Everything Can Feel Harder
Too little sleep—or poor-quality sleep—can contribute to:
Sometimes these symptoms can look remarkably similar to psychiatric symptoms.
That doesn't mean mental health problems are "just poor sleep."
It means sleep and mental health influence each other.
ADHD and sleep problems frequently travel together.
Difficulty transitioning away from stimulating activities, losing track of time, racing thoughts, delayed sleep schedules, and procrastinating bedtime can all interfere with sleep.
Then sleep deprivation can make the next day's:
attention • working memory • impulse control • emotional regulation • motivation
ADHD symptoms staying up late inadequate sleep worse executive functioning → → → → harder day staying up late again →
If you're taking ADHD medication, sleep is also something we'll monitor when deciding whether the medication, dose, and timing are working well for you.
Depression can look very different from person to person.
Others sleep for long periods and still don't feel rested.
Anxiety can make the body tired while the brain remains wide awake.
"I'm exhausted, but my brain won't stop."
Improving sleep doesn't automatically cure depression or anxiety, but persistent sleep problems can make recovery more difficult.
Changes in sleep deserve particular attention for people with bipolar disorder.
Needing significantly less sleep without feeling tired can sometimes be an early sign of hypomania or mania.
That's different from having insomnia and desperately wishing you could sleep.

If you have bipolar disorder and suddenly need much less sleep than usual while experiencing increased energy, activity, impulsivity, irritability, or unusually elevated mood, contact your mental health provider.
Sleep can be difficult during recovery from alcohol or other substances.
The brain and body may need time to re-establish normal sleep patterns, and using another substance simply to force sleep can create additional problems.
If you're struggling with sleep during recovery, tell us.
Poor sleep is something to treat—not something you simply have to endure.
Your brain has an internal timing system called the circadian rhythm.
Light is one of its strongest signals.
This is why sleep isn't only about what you do during the 30 minutes before bedtime.
What you do in the morning and throughout the day matters too.
A reasonably consistent wake time helps anchor your body's clock.
Sleeping dramatically later on days off can sometimes make returning to your normal schedule more difficult.
You don't need perfection. Think consistency rather than rigidity.
Take the dog for a short walk.
Drink your morning coffee on the porch.
Natural outdoor light shortly after waking can help reinforce your circadian rhythm.
Caffeine can remain active in your system for hours.
If you're struggling with sleep, consider not only how much caffeine you consume, but when you consume it.
Remember the caffeine page in this toolkit?
This is one reason it's here.

blocks.text: You Don't Have to Become an Athlete
When people hear "exercise is good for your mental health," it can sound like one more thing they're supposed to be doing.
Movement can support mental health, and it doesn't have to mean joining a gym, running five miles, or following a complicated workout program.
Walking counts. Dancing counts. Gardening counts. Playing with your kids counts.
The best movement is usually something you can actually imagine doing again.
Why Does Movement Help the Brain?
Physical activity affects much more than muscles.
Regular movement can influence systems involved in:
Mood • Stress • Sleep • Attention • Energy • Memory • Motivation • Physical Health
Exercise affects brain signaling and adaptation, including neurotransmitter systems and BDNF (brain-derived neurotrophic factor), a protein involved in the brain's ability to adapt and learn.
Movement can also provide something psychologically important:
Evidence that you can do something difficult.
Sometimes that feeling of accomplishment matters almost as much as the exercise itself.
"I don't have enough energy to exercise."
Unfortunately, doing less can lead to even less energy, less structure, fewer rewarding experiences, and more isolation.
This is why movement can be part of behavioral activation.
Get your body moving for 5 minutes.
Action accomplishment a little more energy more action → → →
Movement can be especially useful for an ADHD brain.
attention • executive functioning • mood regulation • restlessness • stress regulation
Try experimenting with movement before something that requires concentration.
Pay attention to whether getting your body moving changes how easily your brain gets started.
When you're anxious, your nervous system may already feel prepared for action.
Your heart beats faster. Muscles tighten. You may feel restless or "keyed up."
Movement can give some of that physical activation somewhere to go.
For some people, walking, lifting weights, swimming, yoga, cycling, or other movement helps reduce physical tension and makes it easier to settle afterward.
Experiment and notice what yours prefers.
Recovery isn't only about stopping a substance.
routine • reward • connection • confidence • physical health • identity
Movement can become part of that process.
A walking group, recreational sport, hiking club, gym class, or other shared activity can provide both structure and connection.
It doesn't have to become another obsession or another way to punish yourself.
You don't have to exercise alone.
Walking the dog * Playing outside with children
Group fitness * Running or walking clubs
Sometimes the social connection is part of the benefit.
What If I Really Don't Want to Exercise?
"I need to work out for an hour."
After five minutes, you have permission to stop.
If you want to continue, continue.
If you don't, you still succeeded.

Don't commit to changing your entire lifestyle.

Seek medical attention for concerning symptoms such as chest pain, fainting, or severe/unusual shortness of breath with activity.
You don't have to exercise perfectly to benefit from moving your body.

Realistic. Enjoyable—or at least tolerable. Repeatable.

What happened when you tried it?

What you eat and drink can, however, affect:

At Ischys, we're interested in patterns—not perfection.
Before worrying about the newest supplement or superfood, ask:
Am I getting enough protein and nutrient-dense foods?
Am I going most of the day without eating and then crashing later?

blocks.text: Your digestive tract is home to trillions of microorganisms collectively known as the gut microbiome.

Researchers are increasingly interested in the gut-brain axis—the two-way communication system between the digestive tract and the brain. This communication involves the nervous system, immune system, hormones, metabolism, and compounds produced by gut microorganisms.

We're still learning how much changing the microbiome can directly influence specific mental health conditions, so fermented foods shouldn't be considered a treatment for depression, anxiety, ADHD, or other psychiatric disorders.
They can, however, be one part of a varied, nutrient-rich diet.
Fermentation can introduce live microorganisms into certain foods. Examples include:
Yogurt with live and active cultures
Not every product marketed as "fermented" or "probiotic" contains meaningful amounts of live microorganisms by the time you consume it, so check the label when that is your goal.
Don't Forget to Feed the Microbiome
Adding fermented foods is only part of the picture.
Many beneficial gut microorganisms use fiber and other fermentable carbohydrates from foods such as:
Vegetables • Fruits • Beans • Lentils • Whole grains • Nuts • Seeds
Fiber-rich plant foods help provide the environment and fuel for a diverse microbiome.
You don't need an expensive probiotic drink or supplement to begin supporting gut health.
Start With Food When You Can
Instead of immediately purchasing multiple probiotic supplements, consider experimenting with ordinary foods.
Kimchi with rice, eggs, vegetables, or another meal
A fermented food you genuinely enjoy
Some people experience temporary gas or bloating when significantly changing their intake of fermented or high-fiber foods, so gradual changes may be more comfortable.
What About Kombucha and Fermented Drinks?
These can be enjoyable, but check the label.
Depending on the product, fermented drinks may contain varying amounts of:
That can matter if you're monitoring blood sugar, caffeine intake, medications, sleep, pregnancy, or substance-use recovery.
"Good for your gut" doesn't automatically mean unlimited amounts are better.
The gut and brain communicate constantly, and the microbiome appears to be one part of that relationship.
But you don't need to chase the newest "gut health" product.
Eat a variety of plants. Get adequate fiber. Consider fermented foods you enjoy. Make changes gradually.
We're interested in building a healthier overall pattern—not finding one magical food.
Fermented foods and probiotics are not substitutes for treatment of a mental health condition.
Individual dietary recommendations may differ based on medical conditions, medications, pregnancy, immune status, gastrointestinal disorders, allergies, and other factors.

blocks.text: Mental Wellness Isn't Only an Inside Job
We don't all need the same amount of interaction—and being introverted isn't a problem—but meaningful connection and belonging are important parts of mental and physical health.
When mental health becomes difficult, relationships are often one of the first things to change.
"I'll see people when I feel better."
But sometimes isolation becomes part of what keeps us feeling poorly.
Connection Doesn't Mean Having Lots of Friends
You can be surrounded by people and still feel lonely.
And you can have only a few relationships and feel deeply connected.
What matters isn't simply how many people are around you.
Do I have someone I can be myself with?
Do I have someone I can contact when things aren't going well?
Do I feel like I belong somewhere?
Family • Friends • Partners • Neighbors • Coworkers • Faith communities • Support groups •
Clubs • Teams • Classes • Volunteering • Recovery communities • Online communities
Healthy connection can look different for different people.
"Nobody wants to hear about my problems."
"I'll reach out when I'm feeling better."
The problem is that withdrawing can remove some of the very experiences that might help:
conversation • laughter • activity • perspective • affection • accountability • belonging
You don't need to become social overnight.
Sometimes the first step is simply being around another person.
ADHD can affect relationships in ways that have nothing to do with how much you care about someone.
Hyperfocus and disappear into an activity
Experience intense emotions around perceived criticism or rejection Instead of assuming:
"What support would make staying connected easier?"
Calendar reminders, scheduled calls, shared activities, recurring plans, or simply explaining your ADHD to people you trust can sometimes help.
Anxiety Can Make Your World Smaller
Avoidance works incredibly well in the short term.
If a social situation makes you anxious and you cancel, your anxiety usually drops.
Avoiding it made me feel better.
That can make avoidance more likely next time.
Over time, however, your world can become smaller.
When appropriate, gradually approaching safe situations rather than repeatedly avoiding them can help your brain learn:
Substance use disorders thrive in isolation.
Recovery often requires building—or rebuilding—a life that provides:
support • accountability • belonging • purpose • sober activities • people to contact when
There isn't one correct recovery community.
"Who helps me move toward the life I want?"
Connection doesn't mean tolerating relationships that repeatedly harm you.
Healthy relationships generally allow room for:
Respect • Boundaries • Safety • Honesty • Individuality • Repair after conflict
Sometimes improving mental health involves strengthening relationships.
And sometimes it means creating distance from relationships that are unsafe or consistently destructive.
If you're isolated right now, don't start with:
Surrounded by people but still alone
I have someone I can contact when I'm struggling:
The people who help me feel most like myself are:
A relationship I would like to strengthen:
A community where I feel—or might feel—that I belong:
Choose one small action, not a complete social-life makeover.
Eat a meal with another person
Go somewhere instead of staying home
You don't need dozens of relationships.
You need connection that matters to you.
And if you've been isolated for a long time, rebuilding connection may feel uncomfortable before it feels rewarding.
One person. One conversation. One activity. One step toward belonging.

This information is for general education and does not replace individualized mental health treatment. If a relationship involves abuse, threats, coercion, stalking, or immediate danger, individualized safety planning and professional support may be necessary.
You don't have to build recovery alone.
Utah has several community-based resources that can provide peer support, connection, education, recovery activities, and opportunities to meet other people who understand the recovery process.
USARA — Utah Support Advocates for Recovery Awareness
USARA provides peer-based recovery support for individuals and families affected by substance use.
Depending on the program and location, resources may include recovery coaching, support groups, family support, community activities, education, and other recovery services.
You don't have to follow one particular pathway to recovery to seek connection and support.
Learn more: Scan the QR code or visit the USARA resource page provided in the digital version of this toolkit.
The Addiction Recovery Program of The Church of Jesus Christ of Latter-day Saints offers free support meetings based on a 12-step approach combined with Christian and Latter-day Saint principles.
For patients who find strength in faith or would like spiritually oriented recovery support, ARP may provide another source of community, structure, accountability, and connection.
Participation is voluntary, and you do not need to choose a faith-based approach for recovery to be successful.
SMART Recovery • Alcoholics Anonymous (AA) • Narcotics Anonymous (NA) • Al-Anon and
family support • Peer recovery coaching • Group therapy • Individual therapy • Community
The best support system is one that is safe, accessible, meaningful to you, and helps you continue moving toward recovery.
If you aren't sure where to start, ask.
We can help you explore local resources that fit your needs, values, and preferred approach to recovery.
Treatment + Connection + Community can be stronger than trying to do everything alone.

Stress isn't only something you think about.
You can feel it throughout your body:
Racing heart • Tight muscles • Shallow breathing • Upset stomach • Sweating • Restlessness •
Sometimes you know logically that you're okay, but your body hasn't received the message yet.
Learning how to influence that physical response can become another tool in your mental-health toolbox.
Your Nervous System Has Different Gears
When your brain detects stress or threat, your body prepares to respond.
You may move toward a more activated state:
Anxious • Panicky • Angry • Restless • Irritable • Overstimulated • Unable to sit still
Other times, overwhelming stress can look more like:

The goal is to develop more ways to help yourself return toward a manageable state.

Breathe out slowly and a little longer than you breathed in.

blocks.text: Medication Is a Tool—Not the Whole Toolbox
Psychiatric medication can be an important part of treatment.
But medication isn't meant to change who you are.
The goal is to reduce symptoms that interfere with your ability to function, connect, think, sleep, work, learn, recover, and enjoy your life.
At Ischys, medication decisions are something we make with you, not simply for you.
Before starting a medication, you should understand:
2. What symptoms are we hoping it will improve?
3. When might I notice a difference?
4. What common side effects should I watch for?
5. What symptoms mean I should contact my provider?
If you don't know the answers, ask.
Understanding your treatment is part of your treatment.
How Do We Know Whether It's Working?
"Do you think the medication is working?"
Sometimes that's surprisingly difficult to answer.
Getting out of bed more easily.
Those changes often tell us more than simply saying:
Not every psychiatric medication works immediately.
Some effects may appear relatively quickly, while others can take days or several weeks to become clear.
We may also deliberately start with a lower dose and increase gradually.
Starting with more medication isn't automatically better.
Our goal is to find an appropriate dose for you.
If you experience a side effect, tell us.
And don't automatically stop the medication without discussing it with your provider unless you've been given specific instructions to do so or you're experiencing an emergency.
Sometimes a side effect can be addressed by:
Changing the dose • Changing timing • Slowing titration • Treating the side effect • Changing
We can't help troubleshoot something we don't know about.
Taking medication inconsistently can make it difficult to determine whether it's helping.
If remembering medication is difficult, consider:
Pairing medication with an existing routine
Keeping medication somewhere appropriate and visible
If ADHD makes remembering your ADHD medication difficult...
You're definitely not the first person that's happened to.
Let's build a system instead of relying entirely on memory.
Don't Forget Everything Else You're Taking
Some supplements can affect serotonin, sedation, blood pressure, bleeding, liver enzymes, or the way medications are metabolized.
Sleep • Anxiety • Heart rate • Blood pressure • Tremor • Restlessness
This can become particularly important when you're taking medications that affect some of the same systems.
If you suddenly increase from one cup of coffee to several energy drinks per day, tell us.
Depending on your medication, we may monitor things such as:
Blood pressure • Pulse • Weight • Sleep • Appetite • Laboratory values • Movement symptoms
Monitoring doesn't necessarily mean something is wrong.
Please let your provider know about important changes such as:
New or significantly worsening psychiatric symptoms
Another person says a medication was "life-changing."
Someone else says it was terrible.
None of that tells us what your response will be.
Medication response can vary based on:
Diagnosis • Genetics • Metabolism • Other medications • Medical conditions • Age • Sleep •
The goal isn't to reach a particular number.
The goal is the lowest appropriate dose that provides meaningful benefit with acceptable side effects.
Before your next appointment, ask yourself:
How often have I missed a dose?
Have my caffeine, nicotine, alcohol, cannabis, or other substance-use patterns changed?
What question do I want to remember to ask?
You don't need to remember everything.
Screenshots, medication bottles, pharmacy lists, blood-pressure readings, sleep records, and notes on your phone can all help us understand what has happened between appointments.
The more accurate the information, the better decisions we can make together.
And medication is only one part of the larger picture.
"Is treatment helping you live your life better?"

This information is for general education and does not replace individualized medical advice. Do not start, stop, increase, decrease, split, or otherwise change a prescribed medication without following the instructions of your prescribing healthcare professional. Seek urgent or emergency medical care for serious or rapidly worsening symptoms.

Some days are harder than others.
You may wake up feeling depressed, anxious, overwhelmed, irritable, scattered, emotionally exhausted, or simply unable to get started.
On those days, your goal doesn't have to be:
"Make the next hour a little more manageable."
When everything feels wrong, check the basics first.
Used alcohol, cannabis, nicotine, or another substance?
Been scrolling or isolated for hours?
These things don't explain every difficult day.
But they can make a difficult day more difficult.
What is the next small thing?
When thoughts are stuck, change something around your body.
Sometimes changing the environment helps interrupt the loop.
Don't Believe Every Thought You Have on a Bad Day
A difficult emotional state can change how you interpret yourself, other people, and your future.

"Would I see this the same way on one of my better days?"
You don't have to force yourself to think positively.
Just leave room for the possibility that your current state is influencing the story your brain is telling you.
When possible, a highly emotional moment may not be the best time to:
Sleep on it when it is safe to do so.
You can still make the decision later.

Sometimes another person simply being present changes the moment.

When a Hard Day Becomes a Crisis
There is a difference between having a difficult day and being unable to keep yourself or someone else safe.

If you are experiencing suicidal thoughts, thoughts of seriously harming yourself or another person, a potentially life-threatening overdose, severe intoxication, or another immediate safety emergency, get help now.
The 988 Suicide & Crisis Lifeline provides crisis support in the United States.
Call 911 or go to the nearest emergency department
for an immediate medical or safety emergency.
If you're experiencing a substance-related crisis or believe an overdose may have occurred, seek emergency medical assistance.
You do not need to wait for your next appointment when something is urgent.

blocks.text: You Don't Have to Remember Everything
Mental-health treatment doesn't happen only during appointments.
Sometimes you simply need to remember:
"What was that resource we talked about?"
Keep this page somewhere you can find it.
Appointments • Forms • Telehealth visits • Secure communication • Treatment information
Ischys Integrative Mental Wellness Learning Center
Want to learn more about something in this toolkit?
Our online learning center provides additional information about topics such as:
ADHD • Depression • Anxiety • Sleep • Medications • Substance Use & Recovery • Women's
Mental Health • Integrative Mental Wellness • Nutrition • Stress • Lifestyle & Mental Health
You don't need to read everything.
Choose what is relevant to you.
Recovery can involve professional treatment, medication, therapy, peer support, family support, community, spirituality—or a combination.
There is no single pathway that works for everyone.
Utah Support Advocates for Recovery Awareness
Peer-based recovery support, recovery coaching, community resources, activities, and support for individuals and families.
The Addiction Recovery Program of The Church of Jesus Christ of Latter-day Saints provides free, faith-based support using a 12-step framework.
It may be a useful option for people who want spirituality incorporated into their recovery support.
A secular mutual-support approach that emphasizes practical tools for changing behaviors and managing urges.
Community-based mutual-support meetings are available throughout Utah and online.
Ask us if you would like help exploring recovery resources that fit your needs and values.
Substance use, serious mental illness, and other behavioral-health conditions can affect the entire family.
Family members may benefit from education and support too.
Al-Anon • SMART Recovery Family & Friends • NAMI Utah • Family therapy • Peer/family
The National Alliance on Mental Illness Utah provides education, support groups, programs, and resources for individuals and families affected by mental-health conditions.
When You Need More Help Than a Website Can Provide
Online resources and this toolkit are educational.
They aren't substitutes for individualized assessment or treatment.
Contact your healthcare provider when symptoms are worsening, treatment isn't working as expected, you're experiencing concerning medication effects, or something has significantly changed.
Available throughout the United States for people experiencing a mental-health, suicide, or substance-use crisis.
You don't have to be actively suicidal to contact 988.
Call 911 or go to the nearest emergency department for an immediate medical or safety emergency.

For severe symptoms, unconsciousness, difficulty breathing, or another immediate emergency, call 911.
Don't wait until you're having a difficult day.

You don't have to figure everything out yourself.
If you find something online, see something on social media, hear about a supplement, wonder about a medication, or aren't sure whether something applies to you:
Mental wellness isn't built from one perfect decision.
It's usually built from many small things:
Asking for help when you need it
Keep talking with us about what you're learning.
